Intemperate means going well beyond what is reasonable, moderate, or controlled. It describes something — a behavior, a person, a remark, or even a climate — that lacks balance and self-restraint, crossing into excess or extremity.

The easiest way to anchor this word in your mind is through its opposite: temperate. Something temperate is calm, balanced, and measured. Something intemperate is the opposite — it overshoots the reasonable middle ground. Think of a scale. Temperate sits right at the center. Intemperate has tipped heavily to one side.

The word "intemperate" is used in three overlapping but distinct situations:

1. Behavior and Personal Habits (especially overindulgence)

This is the most classic use. An intemperate person lacks self-control in their appetites or habits — they drink too much, eat excessively, or indulge in pleasures without discipline or restraint.

  • His intemperate drinking destroyed his health over the years.
  • She had an intemperate appetite for luxury that quickly put her in debt.

Here, intemperate carries a moral weight. It suggests not just that someone is doing something excessively, but that they should be exercising more self-control and are failing to do so. There is a quiet note of blame or disapproval in the word.

2. Language, Remarks, or Emotional Expression

When someone says something extremely harsh, wildly exaggerated, or explosively angry — going far beyond what the situation warrants — we call that intemperate.

  • The senator's intemperate remarks about immigrants sparked outrage.
  • She sent an intemperate email in the heat of anger, which she later regretted.
  • His intemperate outburst during the meeting embarrassed everyone present.

In this sense, "intemperate" describes speech or emotional expression that is unreasonably fierce, reckless, or disproportionate. A person making intemperate remarks hasn't paused to think, reflect, or moderate themselves — they've let the extreme end of their feelings fly out unchecked.

3. Weather or Climate

This is a more formal, literary use. An intemperate climate or region is one of harsh extremes — brutal winters, scorching summers, violent storms — rather than mild, stable conditions.

  • The explorers were unprepared for the intemperate conditions of the arctic.
  • The region's intemperate winters made farming almost impossible.

This usage is less common in everyday speech but appears in formal writing, history, and literature.
The Single Quality That Unites All Three

Across all three uses, one thing is always true: intemperate describes a failure to stay within reasonable limits. Whether it's a person's habits, their words, or the weather — something intemperate has gone past what is balanced, controlled, or appropriate.
The Emotional Flavor of the Word

"Intemperate" is not a neutral word. It almost always carries a negative or disapproving tone. When you call something intemperate, you are implying that it should have been more controlled, and that the excess is a problem — morally, socially, or practically. It is a word of criticism, not just description.

It also tends to feel slightly formal or elevated. You might read it in a newspaper, a novel, a speech, or a serious discussion. In casual conversation, people might instead say "out of control," "over the top," or "unreasonable" — but intemperate says all of that with more precision and a more serious tone.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Excessive simply means "too much." It is neutral and factual. Intemperate adds the layer of self-control failing and implies moral or social judgment.
  • Immoderate is very close in meaning — nearly a synonym — but is even more formal and rarely used today.
  • Unrestrained focuses on the absence of restraint, while intemperate focuses on the excess that results from that absence.
  • Extreme describes degree alone. Intemperate describes both the degree and the failure of discipline behind it.

You will most often see "intemperate" paired with these kinds of words:

  • Intemperate language / remarks / comments / attack / outburst — harsh, reckless, or disproportionate things said
  • Intemperate behavior / habits / lifestyle — lack of self-discipline in how one lives
  • Intemperate drinking — a classic, traditional use meaning excessive alcohol consumption
  • Intemperate climate / weather / conditions — harsh, extreme natural environment

Intemperate = lacking moderation, self-control, or balance; excessively extreme in behavior, words, or conditions — in a way that is generally disapproved of.

If you ever see the word and feel uncertain, ask yourself: "Is this describing something that has gone well beyond what is balanced or controlled, in a way that seems reckless or problematic?" If yes, intemperate fits perfectly.
